newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Pope appeals for tolerance, ignores threat.
newsitem.headline: Pope appeals for tolerance, ignores threat.

text.p: Pope John Paul, brushing aside an apparent threat to his life in Sarajevo, appealed for peaceful dialogue among Bosnia's wartime religious foes on Sunday.
Only hours before the Roman Catholic leader's arrival on Saturday, police removed explosives planted on his motorcade route into the predominantly Moslem city.
Twenty-three anti-tank mines and plastic explosives attached to a remote control system were found under a main boulevard.

Police said the mines were probably planted on Friday night but there was no indication of who was responsible for the apparent plot to kill the Pope, who narrowly escaped death when he was shot by a Turkish gunman in St Peter's Square in 1981.

Chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said the Pope declined a NATO offer to fly him by helicopter from the airport to the city centre so he would not have to travel in his glass-topped popemobile.
"The Pope said, 'No, I wouldn't even think of it'. He wanted to take the popemobile because it was important to see the people," Navarro-Valls told reporters.

The Pope, prevented from visiting Sarajevo during the war because Serbs refused to guarantee his safety, met Moslem, Croat and Serb members of the new collective presidency on Sunday morning amid tight security.
NATO helicopters flew low over the city and Bosnian authorities deployed thousands of policemen as part of elaborate security precautions.
The 76-year old Pontiff, in declining health, used a cane to make his way up steps before shaking hands with the presidency members.

Speaking at the national museum building which still bears scars from the 1992-95 war, the Pope urged the leaders to build dialogue among Bosnian Moslems, Catholic Croats and Orthodox Christian Serbs.
"Dialogue must be conducted with respect for equality of rights, guaranteed to individual citizens by appropriate legal means, without preference or discrimination," the Pope said.
The peacetime inter-ethnic government has been plagued by political stalemate with politicians from each community unable to agree on the most basic issues.

The Pope held separate meetings with each presidency member, including the Serb representative, Momcilo Krajisnik. The hardline nationalist declined on security grounds to attend Saturday's welcoming ceremony at the airport.
Serb leaders resent the Vatican for its early recognition of the breakaway republics of Croatia and Bosnia during the fighting which accompanied the breakup of the old Yugoslav federation.
Earlier, the Pope held 20 minutes of talks with Metropolitan Nikolaj of the Serbian Orthodox church, who greeted the Pope warmly.
"Have you had time to rest? ...I hope things go well," Nikolaj said.

Thousands of Catholics carrying yellow and white Vatican banners walked through the city to Kosevo soccer stadium on Sunday morning to attend a scheduled open-air mass, the highlight of the Pope's historic visit.
Several hundred buses ferried pilgrims from across Bosnia and neighbouring Croatia to see the Pope, who decided to make the historic trip despite his declining age and safety concerns.
A NATO spokesman said the buses passed through Moslem-controlled territory without incident.
The Papal visit came at a time of tense relations inside the country's Moslem-Croat Federation, which together with a Serb republic comprises postwar Bosnia.
